articles.titulo: Protocol for measuring antibody-dependent enhancement and neutralization using reporter virus particles.
articles.autores: Sheetz A, Frey N, … Doranz BJ (4 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Reporter virus particles (RVPs) are non-replicative, antigenically equivalent viral particles that enable BSL-2-compliant virology research using standard optical detection instrumentation. Here, we present a protocol for measuring neutralization and antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE) of flavivirus infection using dengue virus (DENV) RVPs. For both neutralization and ADE assays, we describe the steps for preparing sera and antibodies, pre-incubating with RVPs to allow immune complex formation, applying to BHK DC-SIGN or K562 cells, and quantifying reporter signal as a readout of viral entry. For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Grinyo-Escuer et al.1.

articles.titulo: HIV proteins disrupt a network of phosphatidylinositol (4,5)-bisphosphate binding sites on the dopamine transporter to regulate amphetamine behaviours.
articles.autores: Zhu Y, Parwana D, … Galli A (13 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Amphetamine (AMPH) use has been linked to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) transmission because HIV can spread through unprotected sex that is associated with AMPH use disorder (AUD). Thus, AUD and HIV have been termed a double epidemic. In this bidirectional relationship, the role played by AUD in HIV-dependent neuropathogenesis is well documented. By contrast, how HIV infection regulates the development of AUD remains elusive. In rodents, expression of HIV viral proteins, such as the trans-activator of transcription (Tat), enhances AMPH escalation (i.e. a progressive intensification of drug use), a Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5) criteria for addiction. In humans, HIV infection increases AMPH frequency of use, as well as the total amount used. Thus, it is possible that HIV/HIV proteins promote the progression of AUD. AMPH-associated behaviours stem, at least in part, from the ability of AMPH to reverse the dopamine (DA) transporter (DAT) function, causing non-vesicular DA release (NVDR) and an increase in extracellular DA. Previously, we provided the first evidence that specific domains of DAT engage in direct association with the plasma membrane lipid, phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2). These interactions are essential for AMPH-induced NVDR and specific behaviours. HIV Tat is a protein that binds PIP2 through its basic domain. We demonstrate that Tat impairs NVDR by disrupting the network of PIP2 binding sites on DAT. Our study provides an atomic scale mechanistic description on how Tat disrupts human DAT/PIP2 association and blunts AMPH-induced NVDR. Using Drosophila as an animal model, we show that Tat by blunting NVDR in the setting of AUD promotes AMPH escalation. KEY POINTS: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) trans-activator of transcription (Tat) impairs non-vesicular dopamine (DA) release (NVDR) by disrupting the network of PIP2 binding sites on human Da transporter (DAT). Our study provides an atomic scale mechanistic description on how Tat disrupts human DAT/phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate association and blunts amphetamine (AMPH)-induced NVDR. We associate Tat blunting of NVDR to the ability of Tat to foster AMPH escalation, using Drosophila as an animal model.
consultas: Stork: S5 (drosophila OR Aedes) AND (virus OR immunity)

articles.titulo: Reshaping the immunometabolic microenvironment via an inflammation-responsive magnesium delivery system to tackle bone diseases.
articles.autores: Li X, Shao H, … Qin L (10 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Recent advancements in magnesium (Mg)-based biomaterials have illuminated their role in immunomodulation. However, their effects on bone repair amid excessive inflammation have not been systematically explored. In this study, we demonstrate that magnesium ions (Mg2+) enhance bone turnover and counteract inflammatory bone loss in a lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced model. Mechanistically, Mg2+ improves mitochondrial metabolic efficiency in bone-forming cells, thereby mitigating oxidative stress caused by excessive inflammation and promoting cell survival. Consequently, the suppression of osteogenic differentiation is effectively reversed under excessive inflammatory conditions. Moreover, Mg2+ modulates the inflammatory microenvironment by enhancing the mitochondrial metabolism of macrophages under oxidative stress. This process facilitates M2 macrophage polarization and stimulates the production of reparative cytokines, such as BMP2, which in turn supports osteogenesis. Furthermore, Mg2+ significantly reduces mitochondrial respiration in osteoclasts and inhibits osteoclastogenesis. We further developed a reactive oxygen species (ROS)-responsive Mg2+ delivery system that specifically targets inflammation-damaged cells and significantly enhances fracture healing under inflammatory conditions. Collectively, our findings highlight the potential of Mg-based biomaterials in the treatment of inflammatory bone diseases.

articles.titulo: Ecological drivers and spatiotemporal dynamics of Opisthorchis viverrini transmission in Southern Laos.
articles.autores: Revolteado MJ, Valencia J, … Sato M (10 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Opisthorchis viverrini remains a persistent public health problem in the Lower Mekong region, where transmission continues despite long-standing control efforts. Effective surveillance requires approaches capable of detecting environmental contamination and capturing temporal and ecological variation in transmission. We assessed the utility of environmental DNA (eDNA) for detecting O. viverrini and examined its ecological and spatiotemporal associations across freshwater systems in Champasak Province, southern Lao PDR. Water samples were collected from four endemic villages at four timepoints between May 2024 and February 2025. O. viverrini eDNA detection was assessed in relation to water physicochemical parameters, water source, village, and the presence of Bithynia spp., the first intermediate snail host. Generalized estimating equations (GEE), with site as the clustering variable, were used to assess associations while accounting for repeated observations within sites. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis provided an exploratory estimate of apparent model discrimination. Bithynia spp. presence was significantly associated with O. viverrini eDNA detection (OR = 3.15, 95% CI: 1.08-9.14; p = 0.035). Sampling timepoint was also associated with detection (p < 0.001). Compared with February 2025, the adjusted odds of detection were lower in May 2024 (OR = 0.013, 95% CI: 0.003-0.070) and August 2024 (OR = 0.061, 95% CI: 0.013-0.278), while the October 2024 contrast was not statistically significant (OR = 0.283, 95% CI: 0.074-1.080; p = 0.065). The fitted model had an apparent AUC of 0.833 (95% CI: 0.778-0.888), an exploratory estimate of discrimination in the analyzed dataset. O. viverrini eDNA detection was associated with Bithynia spp. presence and varied across sampling timepoints, indicating temporal and ecological heterogeneity in environmental occurrence. These temporal associations should be interpreted cautiously because site availability varied between sampling periods and spatial autocorrelation between sites was not explicitly modeled. Environmental eDNA may complement conventional surveillance by helping prioritize sites for further ecological and epidemiological investigation, but detection alone does not establish active local transmission or quantify transmission intensity.

articles.titulo: Vector-Borne Disease Education and Outreach in Arizona: A Qualitative Study of Stakeholder Perspectives.
articles.revista: The American journal of tropical medicine and hygiene
articles.autores: Finucane S, Robinson J, … Yeo S (6 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Successful public health messaging and education can reduce transmission of vector-borne diseases through improved identification and reporting of vectors, reduction in vector habitats, and increased use of personal protective measures. However, it is unclear how Arizona public health and vector control professionals perceive the effectiveness of their current dissemination strategies. We conducted 18 key informant interviews with health department and vector control professionals across Arizona to evaluate current dissemination messaging, materials, and channels and to identify key gaps and challenges. Results indicated that messaging primarily focused on mosquito-borne disease prevention, emphasizing source reduction and personal protective behaviors, and the Fight the Bite campaign was frequently cited. Education on disease symptoms, care-seeking behaviors, and tick-specific risks and prevention practices was less commonly reported. Handouts and flyers were the most common materials, primarily available in English and Spanish. One-on-one interactions and social media were viewed as the most successful dissemination channels. Outreach typically occurred during the monsoon season and in response to positive human cases and vectors. Major challenges included limited funding, staffing constraints, and low public risk perception. Future dissemination should prioritize creating engaging, locally relevant content and adapting strategies to effectively reach the local community. County health departments should also expand education on locally relevant tick-borne diseases, such as Rocky Mountain spotted fever. These findings highlight barriers and opportunities to strengthen public health messaging and dissemination for vector-borne diseases within Arizona.

articles.titulo: Rethinking type 2 diabetes: a bone marrow disease under metabolic disguise?
articles.autores: Fantuzzi F, Spigoni V, … Dei Cas A (9 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) is traditionally viewed as a metabolic disorder driven by insulin resistance and progressive pancreatic β-cell failure. This review examines how metabolic stress remodels the bone marrow (BM) niche and whether these alterations contribute to inflammatory haematopoiesis, defective vascular repair and disease progression. The BM niche is a specialized microenvironment integrating endothelial, mesenchymal, neural, adipocytic, and immune components that cooperatively regulate hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell (HSPC) maintenance, mobilization and immune homeostasis. Evidence from animal models, together with more limited human observations, indicates that obesity-associated inflammation, lipotoxicity and hyperglycaemia can alter these compartments, favour myeloid-biased haematopoiesis and induce persistent metabolic and epigenetic reprogramming. The resulting inflammatory myeloid output may subsequently amplify adipose-tissue and pancreatic islet inflammation, while vascular and autonomic niche dysfunction may constrain endogenous repair, creating bidirectional feedback between systemic metabolic dysfunction and the BM. We integrate these processes within diabet(ogen)ic nicheopathy, a proposed research framework encompassing BM alterations that may arise from and potentially reinforce metabolic disease. Particular attention is given to BM adipose tissue, BM-pancreas inflammatory crosstalk, progenitor mobilopathy and the therapeutic implications of BM programming. However, whether BM alterations precede overt T2D, contribute independently to its progression or predominantly reflect cumulative metabolic injury remains unresolved. The BM niche should therefore be regarded as an emerging mechanistic and therapeutic target rather than an established determinant of T2D progression.

articles.titulo: Live Imaging of Axon Growth in the Developing Drosophila Wing.
articles.autores: Saha S, Forghani R, Giniger E (3 autores)
articles.resumo_original: This protocol describes reproducible, high-resolution imaging of the growth of a single, identified pioneer axon in a developing animal. It uses the well-characterized TSM1 axon of the Drosophila wing to track morphological and cytoskeletal dynamics, as well as signaling processes for which fluorescent markers are available. Between 9 h and 12 h after puparium formation (APF), TSM1 grows nearly 120 µm and undergoes pathfinding to fasciculate with the central L3 nerve of the wing, distal to the guidepost GSR neuron. Imaging of TSM1 in wild-type tissue and following genetic or pharmacological perturbation has revealed morphological parameters of growth cone dynamics and demonstrated how signaling molecules, including the tyrosine kinase Abelson (Abl) and the actin polymerase Enabled (Ena), regulate actin organization within the growth cone. These molecules influence axon growth by redistributing actin mass, supporting filopodial protrusion, and promoting axon extension. In addition to cytoskeleton-dependent growth, recent studies have examined the effects of non-cytoskeletal factors, including NAD+ and Ca2+/calmodulin, on axon growth and branching. Although the precise mechanisms underlying axon growth and guidance remain incompletely understood, this in vivo imaging approach, combined with super-resolution microscopy, provides a platform for identifying additional pathways that regulate them.

articles.titulo: A single-cell transcriptomic atlas of paper wasp brains highlights Kenyon cells' role in social behavior.
articles.revista: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
articles.autores: Behrens C, Chatterjee M, … Sheehan MJ (6 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Social insects provide unique opportunities for studying social interactions, but the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying these behaviors are poorly understood. Here, we performed single-cell sequencing to profile the transcriptomes of 96,310 cells across four phenotypes of Polistes fuscatus paper wasps: foundresses, workers, gynes, and males, to determine how social states and social interactions are encoded in the physiology of the central brain. We characterized the cellular diversity of the Polistes brain and demonstrate that a substantial portion of the brain is composed of diverse populations of Kenyon cell neurons. The composition and gene-expression profiles of these Kenyon cells, as well other neural and non-neural cell populations, vary across sex, caste, and season. We also demonstrate that social interactions, and even the mere observation of a social interaction, induce significant transcriptomic responses, including signatures of neural activation, across populations of Kenyon cell neurons. Notably, the transcriptional and activational signatures elicited by observing a social interaction frequently overlapped with those induced by direct social interaction, suggesting that a shared neural program underlies both direct social interactions and social observation.

articles.titulo: Non-falciparum malaria and the blind spot of HRP2 based rapid diagnostic tests: a nationally representative PCR study of children in the 2024-25 Uganda Malaria Indicator Survey.
articles.autores: Nantalaga KC, Nantege A, Nabirye M (3 autores)
articles.resumo_original:
Malaria diagnosis in Uganda rests almost entirely on rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) detecting histidine rich protein 2 (HRP2), an antigen expressed only by Plasmodium falciparum. Infections with non-falciparum species are therefore invisible to the national testing algorithm by design. Using a subsample of 466 children from the 2013-14 Democratic Republic of the Congo Demographic and Health Survey, Doctor and colleagues concluded that the risk of missing infections through falciparum-specific RDT use was low, but that conclusion rested on only eight non-falciparum mono-infections. No nationally representative estimate exists for Uganda.
We analysed the 2024-25 Uganda Malaria Indicator Survey, in which children aged 6 to 59 months were tested by HRP2 based RDT and by real time PCR with species determination. We estimated survey-weighted prevalence of each species, alone and in mixed infection, and calculated RDT sensitivity separately for P. falciparum mono-infections, mixed infections containing P. falciparum, and non-falciparum mono-infections.
Among 6975 children, weighted parasite prevalence by PCR was 17.5% (95% confidence interval (CI) 15.6 to 19.4). Non-falciparum species were involved in 2.72% (95% CI 2.25 to 3.19) of children and were the sole species in 1.03% (95% CI 0.75 to 1.30). Weighted prevalence of mono-infection was 0.69% (95% CI 0.47 to 0.90) for P. malariae, 0.30% (95% CI 0.14 to 0.46) for P. ovale, and 4 of 6,975 children (exact 95% CI 0.016 to 0.147%) for P. vivax. RDT sensitivity was 82.3% (95% CI 80.0 to 84.6) for P. falciparum mono-infections and 90.7% (95% CI 84.6 to 95.0) for mixed infections containing P. falciparum, but only 14.3% (95% CI 7.1 to 24.7) for non-falciparum mono-infections. Of 267 PCR confirmed infections missed by the RDT, 60 (22.5%) were non-falciparum mono-infections.
Approximately one Ugandan child in a hundred carries a malaria infection that HRP2 based RDTs cannot detect, and such infections account for more than a fifth of all infections the RDT misses. Our estimates confirm, with nearly nine times as many events, the direction of previous findings from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, but they place the absolute burden in a national context that the earlier subsample could not support. This is a structural limitation of the diagnostic, not a failure of test quality, and it will not be resolved by improving HRP2 test performance.

articles.titulo: Development, Characterization and Evaluation of a Stable Eucalyptus globulus Essential Oil-Permethrin Nanoemulsion with Repellent Activity Against Aedes aegypti.
articles.autores: Firoozfar F, Fatemi M, … Moosa-Kazemi SH (9 autores)
articles.resumo_original:
Aedes aegypti is a primary vector of several clinically significant arboviruses. This study aimed to develop a nanoemulsion-based co-delivery system incorporating permethrin and Eucalyptus globulus essential oil for mosquito repellent applications.
The essential oil composition of E. globulus was determined using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS). Nanoemulsions were formulated using a low-energy spontaneous emulsification method and characterized for stability, droplet size distribution and zeta potential. The optimal formulation was further examined by transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and evaluated for cytotoxicity. The repellent activity of eucalyptus essential oil, permethrin, their combinations, and the eucalyptus essential oil-permethrin nanoemulsion was assessed against female Ae. aegypti mosquitoes using the arm-in-cage assay.
The nanoemulsions exhibited a mean droplet size of 93.5 nm and a zeta potential of 60-70 mV, indicating good stability. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) confirmed the presence of spherical and uniformly dispersed droplets. The eucalyptus essential oil-permethrin nanoemulsion demonstrated strong repellency. A 3% permethrin concentration in the eucalyptus-permethrin nanoemulsion provided the maximum protection rate at 91.8%. In stability testing, the 1.5% version of the same nanoemulsion proved to be the most stable.
Eucalyptus globulus essential oil, especially in nanoemulsion form and combined with permethrin, shows promise as a natural repellent formulation against Ae. aegypti. However, field trials are essential to confirm these findings under natural conditions.

articles.titulo: Gut permeability and endotoxemia in obesity.
articles.autores: Fajkić A, Belančić A, … Lam YW (4 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Obesity is increasingly recognized as an immunometabolic disorder in which chronic low-grade inflammation is sustained by persistent upstream triggers rather than by adiposity alone. A central candidate trigger is intestinal barrier dysfunction with metabolic endotoxemia, defined as chronic, subclinical elevations of gut-derived microbial components, most notably lipopolysaccharide (LPS), in the absence of overt infection. In obesity, the intestinal barrier shifts toward increased functional permeability through coordinated remodeling of tight junction organization, mucus layer destabilization, and epithelial stress responses. This creates permissive conditions for microbial ligand passage while mucosal architecture can remain grossly intact. Importantly, systemic exposure is not determined solely by permeability, but by a coupled system involving luminal LPS availability, lipid-facilitated epithelial uptake and export, and context-dependent partitioning and clearance of LPS through binding proteins, lipoproteins, and hepatic handling. Low-dose, repeated LPS signaling engages innate immune pathways (including TLR4 and inflammasome-associated programs), amplifying cytokine production and stress kinase activity that impairs insulin signaling across metabolic tissues. The resulting organ crosstalk within the gut-liver-adipose axis helps explain heterogeneity in metabolic trajectories among individuals with comparable body mass index, particularly when visceral adiposity and postprandial lipid flux are considered. Therapeutic strategies that converge on this axis, including dietary fiber enrichment, microbiota-targeted interventions, metabolic pharmacotherapy, and bariatric procedures, provide proof of reversibility, yet human evidence remains limited by methodological heterogeneity and incomplete causal inference. Advancing the field will require standardized, dynamic barrier phenotyping, longitudinal designs, and stratified intervention trials to identify gut-driven subgroups and enable precision approaches to obesity-related cardiometabolic disease.

articles.titulo: The gut microbiota of Brandt's vole under varying population densities reveals contrasting patterns in the natural environment.
articles.autores: Hilal MG, Tang K, … Wang D (9 autores)
articles.resumo_original:
The population density of rodents fluctuates due to intrinsic and extrinsic factors, inducing density-dependent effects on organisms and their habitats. The gut microbiota of herbivores plays a pivotal role in digestion, immunity, environmental adaptation, and host fitness. Crowding and host population density are considered among the driving factors that influence the gut microbiome of rodents. In laboratory settings, the gut microbiome of Brandt's voles exhibits distinct responses to density and crowding, which is a controlled environment and cannot mimic the natural system; however, its response in natural settings remains underexplored, which is more complex and shaped by biotic and abiotic interactions. Our study provides a comprehensive profiling of the (Lasiopodomys brandtii) gut microbiome at various population densities, under natural conditions, where diet and social structure fluctuate dynamically.
Across all densities, the dominant bacterial phyla were Firmicutes, Bacteroidota, Desulfobacterota, Campylobacterota, Actinobacteriota, and Patescibacteria. The Patescibacteria were significantly lower at medium (0.57% ± 0.117) and high densities (0.65% ± 0.423) than at low density (0.93% ± 0.339), whereas the Proteobacteria were higher at medium density (0.84% ± 0.518) than at low (0.43% ± 0.18) and high (0.54% ± 0.34) densities. Clostridia_vadinBB60 and F082 were reduced at high density relative to low and medium densities, and Lactobacillus abundance was lower at medium density compared with low and high densities. The microbial biomarkers at each density were (p < 0.05, LDA > 3): (Low; Bacilli, Helicobacter, Clostridiales_vadinBB60, F082, and Saccharimonadia), (Medium; Christensenellaceae), (High; Lactobacillus, Prevotella, and Lachnospiraceae). Alpha diversity was significantly lower at high density than at low and medium densities. At high density, Pielou's evenness, Shannon diversity index, observed richness, and Simpson's diversity were significantly lower than at low and medium densities (p < 0.05). Community structure differed significantly between low and high densities and between medium and high densities, but was similar between low and medium densities (p < 0.05). Bacterial predicted functional pathways varied significantly between low and medium densities and between high and medium densities, but showed no differences between low and high densities (p < 0.05). Density, AP, and pH were primary drivers of variance in microbial communities (p < 0.05). Mantel tests show that gut microbial diversity of voles is significantly correlated with density (r = 0.26, p = 0.0006) and water content (r = 0.19, p = 0.025), and microbial abundance is associated with soil water content (r = 0.26, p = 0.001) and aboveground biomass (AGB) (r = 0.24, p = 0.001). Density negatively affects microbial communities while positively affecting the soil physicochemical factors.
This study demonstrates that host population density serves as the primary driver of variation in gut microbiome in wild Brandt's voles. Soil properties and plant biomass act as secondary environmental filters. This work underscores the central role of host population dynamics in shaping the gut microbiome in natural systems, with potential implications for understanding how crowding stress influences host-microbe interactions in wild small mammals.

articles.titulo: Sanghuang polysaccharides as emerging immunomodulators: linking molecular structure, immune recognition and the gut microbiota-immune axis.
articles.autores: Ma X, Chen X, … Gong N (6 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Sanghuang - a group of medicinal polypores now taxonomically reassigned from Phellinus linteus sensu lato to the genus Sanghuangporus - has been used for two millennia in East Asian medicine, and its polysaccharides are now recognized as the principal immunologically active constituents. Yet the field remains fragmented: "Sanghuang polysaccharide" is not a single molecule but a structurally heterogeneous family of β-glucans, heterogalactans, mannans and polysaccharide-protein complexes whose immune effects may be governed by the coupling of molecular structure × pattern-recognition receptor × cell type × host microenvironment. This review synthesizes current evidence across five layers - chemical structure, immune recognition, innate and adaptive cellular immunomodulation, immunometabolic regulation and the potential for trained immunity, and the gut microbiota-immune axis - and maps them onto immune-mechanism-based applications spanning tumor immune-microenvironment remodeling, barrier immunity and microbiota-associated regulation, host defense and inflammatory resolution, and immunometabolic disorders. We critically grade the receptor evidence, showing that most Sanghuang studies remain correlative (pathway phosphorylation or cytokine readouts) rather than demonstrating direct receptor engagement, in contrast to the benchmark fungal β-glucans lentinan, schizophyllan and PSK/Krestin, for which Dectin-1, Toll-like receptor and complement receptor 3 mechanisms are established. We further examine oral bioavailability and pharmacokinetic constraints that shape whether luminal, gut-associated lymphoid or systemic mechanisms dominate. We propose a minimum reporting standard (Box 1) covering species authentication, extraction and purity control (including endotoxin and protein/phenolic contamination), structural characterization and receptor validation, and outline a multi-omics- and AI-enabled roadmap to move the field from asking "is it effective?" to "which structure, via which receptor, in which cell and which disease context?". Sanghuang polysaccharides therefore emerge as context-dependent immunomodulators rather than universal immune stimulants, and they represent a tractable model system for structure-defined fungal immunomodulators - but translation requires rigorous standardization and mechanistic validation.

articles.titulo: A nationally representative One Health multi-pathogen serosurvey in Cambodia: study protocol for the RACSMEI mixed-methods study.
articles.autores: Antoniolli A, Karlsson E, … Flamand C (41 autores)
articles.resumo_original:
Cambodia faces a high and complex burden of zoonotic, vector-borne, vaccine-preventable and environmentally transmitted infections, driven by intensive human-animal-environment interactions. However, nationally representative data integrating human, animal and environmental dimensions of pathogen exposure remain limited. The RACSMEI (Risk Assessment of Community Spread of Multiple Endemic Infectious Diseases in a One Health Perspective) study aims to address this gap through a nationwide One Health serosurvey designed to generate policy-relevant epidemiological evidence for precision public health and integrated surveillance.
RACSMEI is a nationwide, cross-sectional, mixed-methods study conducted across all 25 provinces of Cambodia. Using a stratified, multi-stage cluster sampling design, approximately 15,000 individuals aged 2-75 years will be enrolled from 4,160 households in 104 randomly selected villages. Human, animal (poultry, pigs, dogs, cattle, small ruminants, rodents) and environmental (water, soil, air, surface swabs) samples will be collected. Exposure to more than 50 endemic, emerging, vaccine-preventable and elimination-targeted pathogens will be assessed using multiplex serological assays, molecular diagnostics and metagenomics sequencing approaches. Quantitative surveys will be complemented by semi-structured interviews and focus group discussions to explore social, behavioural and health system determinants of infection risk and care-seeking behaviours. Analyses will account for the complex survey design and integrate epidemiological, environmental and social science data.
By combining nationally representative sampling with integrated human, animal, environmental and social science data, RACSMEI aims to generate comprehensive evidence on infectious disease exposure and transmission risks across diverse socio-ecological contexts in Cambodia. The study will provide policy-relevant insights to support One Health surveillance strategies and targeted public health interventions. The protocol was approved by the Cambodian National Ethics Committee for Health Research and the Institutional Review Board of Institut Pasteur Paris.
The study is registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT07358910). It was retrospectively registered on 14 January 2026.

articles.titulo: Applications of computer vision in mosquito-borne diseases: A systematic review.
articles.autores: Ong SQ, Brkljač B, … Hackenberger BK (8 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Mosquito-borne diseases (MBDs) remain a major global health challenge. Vector surveillance, pathogen detection, and clinical diagnosis are central to control efforts but are limited by labor-intensive workflows and shortages of trained personnel. Computer vision (CV) offers opportunities for scalable automation throughout the MBD management pipeline. We aimed to systematically characterize the applications of computer vision in mosquito-borne diseases research, summarize methodological developments, and identify opportunities and barriers to translating these advances into public health practice. We conducted a systematic review in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines, searching PubMed, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore for studies published between January 1, 2010, and December 31, 2025, that applied computer vision to any aspect of MBD research or control. A total of 1,521 records were screened, and 650 studies met the inclusion criteria. Studies were categorized by computer vision application area, data types, algorithmic approaches, and data acquisition methods. Descriptive quantitative analysis and qualitative thematic synthesis were performed. The use of computer vision in MBD research increased significantly over the review period. Most studies focused on diagnostic applications, particularly Plasmodium detection in malaria microscopy. More recent work incorporated deep learning models for mosquito species classification, UAV- and satellite-based habitat mapping, and smartphone-based non-invasive diagnostic imaging. Emerging areas included 3D mosquito behavioral analysis and Internet of Things-enabled surveillance. Algorithmic approaches evolved from traditional image processing to convolutional neural networks, You Only Look Once (YOLO)-based object detectors, and transformer architectures. However, most models were developed using small, geographically-limited datasets, lacked external or prospective validation, and were rarely evaluated in operational settings, limiting their translational readiness.

articles.titulo: Intestinal Xdh overexpression promotes organismal aging with early redox dysregulation.
articles.autores: Pan S, Zhang F, … Li Y (11 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Oxidative stress accompanies aging, but whether a defined endogenous oxidant source can initiate tissue-to-organism aging remains unclear. We investigated xanthine oxidase (XO), an enzyme coupling purine catabolism to superoxide and hydrogen peroxide generation, using a human cross-sectional cohort and Drosophila genetic models. Among 442 adults, higher serum XO activity was independently associated with shorter relative leukocyte telomere length. Ubiquitous overexpression of xdh, the Drosophila xanthine oxidoreductase gene, shortened lifespan, accelerated locomotor decline, disrupted metabolic homeostasis, reduced antioxidant enzyme activities, and remodeled redox-, immune-, and metabolism-related transcriptional programs. Intestine-specific xdh overexpression was sufficient to reproduce organismal lifespan shortening and functional decline in both sexes. Intestinal xdh elevation increased intestinal DCF fluorescence and reduced total superoxide dismutase activity before detectable barrier leakage or expansion of culturable intestinal bacteria. These early redox abnormalities were followed by progressive barrier failure, increased bacterial burden, and reduced survival during hydrogen peroxide challenge. Intestinal transcriptomics further revealed early and persistent enrichment of oxidoreductase, glutathione, immune, and lipid-metabolic programs, with shared functional signatures across intestinal xdh overexpression, systemic xdh overexpression, and chronological aging. Collectively, these findings identify intestinal XO as a defined metabolic source of redox disruption capable of producing effects beyond the gut. They support a model in which sustained intestinal oxidative stress precedes and amplifies the loss of gut homeostasis, linking local redox disturbance to organismal aging phenotypes.

articles.titulo: HligTPS-mediated trehalose homeostasis links metabolic reprogramming to cold adaptation in Hylurgus ligniperda.
articles.autores: Cheng L, Han Y, … Tao J (9 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Overwintering adaptation is a critical determinant of whether invasive forest insects can overcome climatic constraints and successfully establish in newly invaded regions. Trehalose, a major cryoprotectant, is widely recognized as playing an essential role in cold adaptation. However, the dynamic regulatory mechanisms governing trehalose metabolism and its functional relationship with cold tolerance remain poorly understood. Here, naturally overwintering populations of Hylurgus ligniperda were used to investigate the role of trehalose-6-phosphate synthase (TPS)-mediated trehalose metabolism in cold adaptation through metabolomic analysis, RNA interference, and exogenous compensation experiments. Metabolomic profiling revealed extensive metabolic reprogramming during overwintering, with carbohydrate metabolism as the most significant enriched pathway. Trehalose accumulation closely paralleled seasonal changes in cold tolerance and peaked during mid-overwintering. The trehalose biosynthetic gene HligTPS was significantly induced during overwintering and under acute cold stress. Silencing HligTPS reduced trehalose content and elevated LT50 (from -8.3 ± 1.1 °C to -6.7 ± 1.0 °C), indicating impaired cold tolerance, whereas exogenous trehalose supplementation partially rescued this phenotype. Notably, moderate trehalose elevation enhanced cold tolerance, whereas excessive accumulation increased mortality. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that carbohydrate metabolic reprogramming contributes to overwintering adaptation and HligTPS-mediated trehalose biosynthesis as a key mechanism underlying cold adaptation in H. ligniperda. More importantly, our results suggest that cold tolerance depends on the maintenance of trehalose homeostasis rather than on trehalose accumulation alone. This study provides new insights into the metabolic basis of insect overwintering adaptation and the climatic adaptability of invasive forest pests.

articles.titulo: Tissue repair and regeneration: molecular mechanisms and therapeutic interventions.
articles.autores: Zhang M, He J, Li Q (3 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Tissue injury is a pervasive feature of human disease, yet adult mammals exhibit limited regenerative capacity. A central determinant of regenerative outcomes is the inflammatory response, which orchestrates tissue repair through mechanisms that are evolutionarily conserved from Drosophila to mammals. Following injury, inflammation drives debris clearance, promotes the release of cytokines and growth factors, and contributes to the restoration of functional cells. However, dysregulated or unresolved inflammation can impair healing, drive scar formation, and ultimately result in organ dysfunction or failure. Here, we focus on recent advances in the spatiotemporal regulation of inflammation during tissue repair that have reshaped our understanding of its underlying mechanisms. We synthesize findings on the dynamic progression of repair from inflammatory initiation to active resolution and stem cell activation, highlighting features of immune cell plasticity and heterogeneity within injury-specific microenvironments, as well as the existence of pivotal macrophage-fibroblast interactions. Furthermore, we delineate the pleiotropic and context-dependent roles of key cytokines and signaling pathways in coordinating these processes. Finally, we discuss current and emerging therapeutic strategies, emphasizing the paradigm shift from broad immunosuppression toward precise modulation of inflammatory networks to promote regeneration and prevent fibrosis. Future progress hinges on integrating multiomic spatial atlases, precision immunomodulation, and standardized therapeutic protocols to decipher and manipulate immune-regenerative crosstalk, thereby driving the development of next-generation regenerative therapies.

articles.titulo: Quantitative Estimation of the Risk of Rift Valley Fever Virus Spread via Legal Livestock Movements From Northeastern KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa
articles.autores: Ngoshe YB, Etter E, … Thompson PN (5 autores)
articles.resumo_original:
Rift Valley fever (RVF) virus (RVFV) is a mosquito-borne zoonotic pathogen with major implications for animal and human health. There have been reports of large RVF outbreaks in the interior of South Africa in the 1950s, the 1970s, and 2010-2011. Northeastern KwaZulu-Natal (KZN), which shares borders with Eswatini and Mozambique, was reported to be a RVF hyperendemic area in 2019, with the detection of RVFV related to the virus responsible for the 1950 outbreak. Frequent livestock movements occur out of this area under permits issued by the state veterinary services.
This study aimed to estimate the probability of RVFV being spread from northeastern KZN to a destination elsewhere in South Africa via legal movement of cattle and goats. Specifically, the monthly risk of at least one viraemic animal arriving at a destination outside the study area was estimated.
A spatial-stochastic risk assessment model was designed to estimate monthly and location-specific risk of RVFV export, following World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) guidelines. The model was run by integrating data from previous studies on the characterisation of domestic ruminant movement patterns and on livestock RVFV seroprevalence and seroconversion rate in cattle and goats reported from the study area. The animal movement data included animal movement permit records (2015-2018) from the KZN Department of Agriculture and Rural Development (KZNDARD) from 94 dip tanks across three ecological areas (mountain, riverine and coastal).
Goats posed the highest probability of contributing to the RVFV spread to a destination location outside the study area. This aligns with their predominance in animal exports across all regions, particularly in the riverine area, which alone accounted for 51.6% of all cattle and goat movements. Temporal modelling showed the peak risk of RVFV viraemic animals arriving at a destination to be during January-March for goats (99%, [2-100]95%) and February for cattle (99%, [2-100]95%), coinciding with increased animal movements and favourable environmental conditions for vector activity. Mountain areas consistently showed low risk. In contrast, the coastal areas presented moderate but variable risk throughout the year. Sensitivity analysis identified incidence rate of RVFV infection per month, the number of animals exported per month, and the duration of viraemia as the parameters in the model that had a strong effect on the variability in the probability of exporting viraemic animals.
There is a high probability of RVFV viraemic animals arriving at destinations elsewhere in South Africa via legal movements from northeastern KZN. The risk was highest from the riverine and coastal areas for cattle and goats, the riverine areas presenting the highest risk of export. The late summer months (February-March) posed the highest threat. Integrating spatiotemporal risk modelling into a One Health surveillance framework could enhance early detection, enable targeted interventions, and reduce the risk of both animal and human RVFV exposure in South Africa. Risk of exposure assessment at arrival is also needed to ultimately estimate the risk of the virus being responsible for outbreaks in other regions of South Africa.

articles.titulo: Beyond Bioassays: Why are Apiaceae-Derived Mosquitocides yet to Reach Vector Control Programs?
articles.revista: Vector borne and zoonotic diseases (Larchmont, N.Y.)
articles.autores: Ojo O, Prinsloo G (2 autores)
articles.resumo_original:
Mosquito-borne diseases remain a major global public health challenge, with their transmission increasingly exacerbated by climate change, urbanization, and the spread of insecticide resistance. Although synthetic insecticides remain central to mosquito control programs, their extensive use has resulted in resistance development, environmental contamination, and adverse effects on nontarget organisms, highlighting the need for safer and more sustainable alternatives. Over the past two decades, medicinal plants of the Apiaceae family have emerged as promising sources of mosquitocidal agents owing to their rich phytochemical diversity and demonstrated larvicidal, ovicidal, adulticidal, and repellent activities against major mosquito vectors, including Aedes, Anopheles, and Culex species.
This review examines recent advances (2021-2026) in the mosquitocidal potential of Apiaceae medicinal plants, with particular emphasis on the translational barriers limiting their progression from laboratory discovery to practical vector control applications.
Current evidence on phytochemical constituents, biological activities, mechanisms of action, and safety considerations is synthesized alongside critical challenges, including chemical variability, inadequate standardization, essential oil instability, formulation constraints, regulatory hurdles, scalability limitations, and the absence of field-based validation. Emerging strategies to improve formulation stability, quality control, and product development are also discussed. Despite a strong and growing body of laboratory evidence, the translation of Apiaceae-derived mosquitocides into commercially viable vector control products remains limited.
Future progress will require multidisciplinary, application-oriented research that integrates formulation science, toxicological assessment, field validation, regulatory readiness, and scalable production systems to bridge the gap between laboratory promise and public health implementation.

articles.titulo: Ultrasound-assisted synthesis of chromene-carbohydrazide hybrids as promising larvicidal agents against Culex pipiens: integrated biological and computational evidence for acetylcholinesterase inhibition and oxidative stress
articles.autores: El-Bana GG, Farag B, … Baz MM (8 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Developing environmentally friendly larvicides with novel modes of action is necessary because insecticide resistance is widespread in mosquito populations. Despite considerable efforts to discover new mosquito control agents, studies integrating biological efficacy, biochemical mechanisms, computational chemistry, and SAR analyses within a single framework remain limited. Here, we assessed a series of chromene-carbohydrazide derivatives (3a-d, 5, and 7) using third-instar Culex pipiens larvae. Each hybrid exhibited significant concentration- and time-dependent larvicidal activity, with compound 3b showing the highest potency (LC₅₀ = 52.43 and 44.26 μg/mL after 24 and 48 h, respectively), followed by 3c and 3d, while compound 5 was the least active. Several derivatives achieved 100% larval mortality at 500 μg/mL, but they were considerably less potent than the reference Temephos (0.25 μg/mL). Biochemical assessments showed significant inhibition of acetylcholinesterase, α- and β-esterases, digestive enzymes, and antioxidant defenses. Protein, carbohydrate, lipid peroxidation, and protein carbonyl contents were also elevated, indicating severe oxidative stress. Toxicity toward non-target organisms was generally low, although Gambusia affinis exhibited notable sensitivity. Density functional theory showed reduced HOMO-LUMO energy gaps and enhanced electrophilicity among the chromene-carbohydrazide derivatives, with 3c displaying the strongest electron-accepting character. Molecular docking and a 100 ns molecular dynamics simulation showed stable binding of 3b within the acetylcholinesterase active gorge, supporting its inhibitory activity. Collectively, these findings establish chromene-carbohydrazide hybrids, particularly 3b, as promising laboratory larvicidal agents whose mode of action involves, at minimum, acetylcholinesterase inhibition and oxidative stress, with additional downstream effects on detoxification and digestive enzymes. However, this study was conducted only under laboratory conditions and did not assess environmental safety, field efficacy, or practical applicability. Future research should prioritize field validation, formulation optimization, and ecotoxicological risk assessment before operational use in vector control programs.

articles.titulo: Emerging Vector-Borne Diseases in North America
articles.autores: Shahbodaghi D, Rathjen N (2 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Vector-borne diseases are a significant and growing public health concern. They account for approximately 20% of infectious diseases globally and cause more than 700,000 deaths each year. These diseases are caused by viral, bacterial, or parasitic pathogens most commonly transmitted through the bites of infected mosquitoes and ticks. In the United States, emerging viral infections include West Nile, dengue, chikungunya, and Zika; emerging bacterial infections include human monocytic ehrlichiosis, human granulocytic anaplasmosis, and Rocky Mountain spotted fever. Bacterial infections often require early recognition and prompt treatment with doxycycline. Increasing incidence of vector-borne diseases is closely linked with environmental changes, climate shifts, urbanization, and increased interaction with vector habitats. Preventive strategies include minimizing skin exposure with appropriate clothing, using insecticide-treated bed nets, and applying insect repellents containing 20% to 30% N, N-diethyl-m-toluamide (DEET) or 20% picaridin. Applying permethrin to clothing provides additional protection. Because many vectors are active during the day-particularly Aedes mosquitoes and most ticks-protective measures should extend beyond nighttime exposure.

articles.titulo: Instance-Wise Contrastive Graph Neural Network Enables the Discovery of Novel Aedes aegypti Larvicidal Compounds
articles.revista: Journal of chemical information and modeling
articles.autores: Lúcio da Costa KS, Caldeira GHG, … Neves BJ (16 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Aedes aegypti remains a major arboviral vector, making larval control a critical strategy to reduce mosquito populations. However, resistance to commercial larvicides has reduced the long-term effectiveness of current interventions, reinforcing the need for new compounds with improved potency and selectivity. Here, we present an instance-wise contrastive graph neural network (GNN) framework to accelerate the discovery of novel larvicidal compounds. The model was trained on a curated data set of 556 organic compounds organized into LC50-derived multitask classification thresholds and integrated Transformer-inspired graph learning with whole-molecule and fragment-level contrastive regularization. This model achieved strong held-out performance, with global AUC = 0.95 ± 0.01, PR-AUC = 0.93 ± 0.01, MCC = 0.77 ± 0.03, and G-mean = 0.88 ± 0.02, outperforming conventional machine learning and graph-based baselines. Predictive uncertainty analysis and counterfactual maps further supported the interpretation of threshold-sensitive predictions and substructural contribution patterns. The model was applied to screen 1.3 million compounds, resulting in 10 candidates for experimental validation. Three compounds showed measurable larvicidal activity against A. aegypti larvae. Among them, LC-79 emerged as the most promising hit, with 2-day and 5-day LC50 values of 0.24 μg/mL (0.66 μM) and 0.05 μg/mL (0.13 μM), respectively, an IE50 of 0.06 μg/mL (0.16 μM), and rapid larval mortality (LT50 = 1.10 days at 1 μg/mL). LC-79 also showed no measurable acute toxicity to Daphnia magna at the highest tested concentration [EC50-48h > 43 μg/mL (> 119 μM)], resulting in selectivity indices > 180 and > 860 relative to its 2-day and 5-day LC50 values. Overall, this study demonstrates that contrastive graph learning can move beyond retrospective larvicide modeling to experimentally validated hit discovery, identifying LC-79 as a potent and preliminarily selective acylthiourea larvicide candidate for further mechanism-of-action, resistance, and semifield evaluation.

articles.titulo: Ecotoxicological Effects and Acetylcholinesterase Inhibition of Piper sarmentosum Hexane Extract in Danio rerio Larvae
articles.autores: Othman AN, Zaidan UH, … Shamsi S (3 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Botanical larvicides are increasingly investigated as alternatives to synthetic insecticides; however, their effects on nontarget aquatic organisms require careful evaluation. Piper sarmentosum hexane extract (PSHE) has previously demonstrated larvicidal activity against Aedes aegypti, but its toxicity to nontarget aquatic organisms remains insufficiently characterized. The present study evaluated the phytochemical composition and acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibitory activity of PSHE and assessed its toxicity to Danio rerio larvae, using temephos (TE) as a reference larvicide. GC-MS analysis identified 12 compounds in PSHE, with (Z)-isoelemicin (44.82%), asarone (35.23%) and myristicin (9.03%) as the major constituents. PSHE inhibited AChE activity in vitro in a concentration-dependent manner, with an IC50 of 17.82 μg/mL (95% CI: 15.56-20.49 μg/mL). Exposure of D. rerio larvae to PSHE resulted in concentration- and exposure-dependent mortality, with LC50 values of 3.93, 1.89, and 0.47 μg/mL at 5, 6, and 7 days post-fertilization (dpf), respectively. Corresponding LC50 values for TE were 20.19, 11.50 and 6.12 μg/mL. PSHE exposure was also associated with reduced motility, altered heartbeat rate, scoliosis, pericardial edema and other morphological abnormalities. These findings demonstrate that PSHE exhibits measurable AChE inhibitory activity and substantial toxicity towards D. rerio larvae under the conditions tested. The results highlight the importance of assessing nontarget toxicity and selectivity when evaluating PSHE for potential development as a botanical larvicidal material.

articles.titulo: Macrophage immunometabolic programming in pulmonary arterial hypertension: prioritizing TET2 and METTL3/m⁶A
articles.autores: Meng H, Liao J, … Deng Y (4 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is sustained by pulmonary vascular remodeling and right ventricular (RV) maladaptation that often remain incompletely reversible despite contemporary pathway-directed therapy. A central mechanistic question is how macrophage states that promote remodeling are maintained. This focused narrative review examines three potentially coexisting explanations: continued conditioning by the pathological niche, selective recruitment of monocyte subsets with pre-existing inflammatory signatures, and cell-intrinsic regulatory states that persist after stimulus withdrawal. Single-cell and spatial studies identify lesion-, subset- and stage-dependent macrophage states, but cannot alone distinguish these explanations. Metabolic regulation of chromatin and RNA provides candidate links between local cues and sustained function. We compare TET2-dependent DNA regulation and METTL3/m6A-dependent RNA fate as complementary routes through which metabolic cues may influence inflammatory restraint and effector output. Human associations and hematopoietic or myeloid perturbation studies support their investigation, but do not establish durable programming in human lesional macrophages. We therefore distinguish ongoing activation from persistent programming and trained immunity, evaluate pulmonary and RV evidence separately, and define the validation requirements for testing whether disruption of macrophage-state maintenance can reverse established disease.

articles.titulo: Time-resolved multi-omics reveals sustained antiviral activation and hepatic lipid remodeling during ALV-J infection in chickens
articles.autores: Chen S, Wang Q, … Chang G (7 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Avian leukosis virus subgroup J (ALV-J) is an oncogenic retrovirus associated with persistent infection, immunosuppression, and neoplastic diseases in chickens, with the liver serving as an important target organ. However, the temporal coordination of hepatic immune and metabolic responses during the early course of ALV-J infection remains unclear. Here, we performed time-resolved proteomic and metabolomic analyses of chicken livers at 7, 14, and 21 days post-infection (dpi). Hepatic ALV-J RNA was detected throughout the observation period and was accompanied by histopathological injury and extensive immunometabolic remodeling. Antiviral and interferon-responsive proteins, including OASL, STAT1, EIF2AK2, and CMPK2, remained elevated at multiple time points. The sustained elevation of these antiviral proteins was accompanied by reductions in selected mitochondrial respiratory-chain proteins and the redox cofactors NADH and flavin mononucleotide. Lipid remodeling also became increasingly prominent over the course of infection, as reflected by the accumulation of multiple lysophospholipid species, together with decreases in phospholipid backbone-related metabolites. Based on its persistent induction and known roles in antiviral responses and mitochondrial nucleotide metabolism, CMPK2 was selected for functional analysis. ALV-J infection induced CMPK2 expression in HD11 cells. CMPK2 overexpression increased intracellular DHE fluorescence, ALV-J Env protein levels, and infectious viral titers, whereas treatment with CMPK2-targeting siRNAs reduced DHE fluorescence without significantly affecting viral replication. These findings suggest that CMPK2 contributes to infection-associated changes in DHE fluorescence in HD11 cells, while its overexpression can enhance ALV-J replication under the tested conditions. Collectively, the early course of ALV-J infection is characterized by sustained antiviral activation accompanied by mitochondrial/redox and hepatic phospholipid remodeling, with CMPK2 representing a potential contributor to the associated oxidative response.

articles.titulo: Balancing Trained Immunity and Tolerance: Innate Immunity Crossroads in COVID-19 Vaccination
articles.autores: Lima-Silva LF, Angelim MKSC, … Moraes-Vieira PM (3 autores)
articles.resumo_original: The COVID-19 pandemic has underscored the critical role of immune responses in determining disease severity, with SARS-CoV-2 infection triggering both protective and pathological reactions. While adaptive immunity (mediated by neutralizing antibodies and memory T cells) has been the primary focus of vaccination strategies, emerging evidence highlights the importance of innate immune adaptation, a spectrum of states ranging from trained immunity, in which innate immune cells undergo epigenetic and metabolic reprogramming, enhancing rapid, broad-spectrum antiviral defenses, to innate immune tolerance, in which persistent stimulation renders the same cells hyporesponsive. In this review, we frame SARS-CoV-2 infection and COVID-19 vaccination as opposing forces along this training-tolerance continuum, and we distinguish three levels of evidence: persistent epigenetic and metabolic marks, altered responses to a secondary challenge, and demonstrable effects on clinical outcomes. We discuss how pattern recognition receptors initiate antiviral responses, how metabolic reprogramming influences immune cell behavior, and how trained immunity extends beyond leukocytes to airway epithelial and endothelial cells. Trained immunity inducers, such as Bacillus Calmette-Guérin vaccination, show promise in preclinical studies but yield mixed clinical results, highlighting the challenges of translating innate immune modulation into therapeutic benefits. We further examine how SARS-CoV-2 itself can act as a natural inducer of trained immunity, how maladaptive resolution of this program may contribute to long COVID, and why only a subset of infected individuals develops post-acute sequelae. Finally, we consider the post-pandemic immunological landscape, including immune debt and the resurgence of unrelated infections due to reduced microbial exposure, and the lessons these hold for vaccines against future emerging respiratory viruses. Future vaccination strategies should aim to promote context-appropriate innate antiviral responses while limiting maladaptive inflammatory persistence, integrating innate immune regulation with durable adaptive protection against SARS-CoV-2 and emerging respiratory pathogens.

articles.titulo: The benefits and pitfalls of trained immunity in listeria monocytogenes-based cancer vaccination: how host innate-cell reprogramming may amplify, distort, or constrain the therapeutic potential of live bacterial vectors
articles.autores: Amarante-Mendes GP, Leão de Freitas MA, … Bortoluci KR (7 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Live recombinant Listeria monocytogenes (Lm) vaccines are usually framed as intracellular antigen-delivery platforms endowed with intrinsic adjuvant activity. Here we argue that this view may be incomplete. Because Lm vaccines strongly engage innate immune cells, their efficacy might depend on both immediate inflammatory signaling and a separately established or acquired trained state. Importantly, direct evidence that recombinant Lm induces bona fide trained immunity - defined by durable functional changes supported by epigenetic and metabolic reprogramming beyond the initial inflammatory phase - is currently limited. We consider two distinct questions: whether pre-existing trained immunity changes the efficacy of subsequent Lm vaccination, and whether Lm vaccination itself induces a lasting trained innate program in addition to antigen-specific CD8 T-cell immunity. Pre-existing training could alter vector clearance, antigen presentation, and initial T-cell priming, whereas hypothetical Lm-induced training could affect later tumor-microenvironment function, memory recall, and long-term tumor control without accounting for the initial CD8 T-cell response. Either scenario might enhance or constrain efficacy, and the two require different experimental examinations. We propose trained innate reprogramming as a testable mechanistic variable, rather than an established property of Lm vaccines, with implications for vaccine design, repeated dosing, safety, and interpretation of antitumor vaccines.

articles.titulo: Innate Immunity in the Oral-Brain Axis: Trained Immunity as a Candidate Link Between Periodontitis and Alzheimer's Disease
articles.autores: Jia Y, Ding J, … Cao Z (6 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a complex neurodegenerative disorder shaped by aging, genetic susceptibility, and environmental factors. Observational studies have associated periodontitis with cognitive impairment and dementia, but its causal contribution to AD remains uncertain. This review examines trained immunity as a potential mechanism through which chronic periodontal inflammation might modify neuroinflammatory susceptibility. Trained immunity refers to persistent functional reprogramming of innate immune cells following an initial stimulus, supported by metabolic and epigenetic remodeling and altered responses to subsequent challenges, and is distinct from inflammatory activation during ongoing periodontitis. Studies suggest that experimental periodontal inflammation can reprogram bone marrow myelopoiesis, and separate studies demonstrate that peripheral inflammatory stimulation can alter microglial memory and amyloid pathology. These findings establish different components of the proposed pathway. However, clinical evidence for periodontitis-associated training is preliminary and inconsistent, and direct demonstration that such training mediates AD biomarker changes or clinical progression is lacking. Therefore, we distinguish human associations, genetic causal-inference studies, periodontal experiments, and mechanisms established in non-periodontal models. Shared risk factors, reverse causation, exposure heterogeneity, and potentially protective or tolerant immune responses provide important alternative interpretations. We propose stimulus-removal experiments, lineage-resolved perturbation studies, and longitudinal human investigations to test persistence and mediation. Supportive periodontal care remains indicated for oral health; its neuroprotective efficacy, oral-fluid biomarkers of AD, and oral-brain prediction models require prospective validation. The framework positions periodontitis as a potential modifier while retaining systemic inflammatory aging and shared susceptibility as competing explanations.

articles.titulo: Hyperuricemia and systemic inflammation synergistically associated with irreversible β-cell bioenergetic collapse and clinical infection vulnerability
articles.revista: Inflammation research : official journal of the European Histamine Research Society ... [et al.]
articles.autores: Su FY, Hsu YH, … You RI (9 autores)
articles.resumo_original:
To investigate the synergistic impact of hyperuricemia and systemic inflammation on clinical infection susceptibility and the mechanisms of pancreatic β-cell bioenergetic failure.
A retrospective clinical cohort analysis evaluated correlations between glycemic status, immuno-metabolic markers, and pathogen risks. Mechanistically, β-cells exposed to uric acid (UA) and cytokines were assessed for real-time bioenergetics, redox proteomics, and cell fate trajectories.
Clinical immuno-metabolic profiling demonstrated progressive elevation of serum uric acid, CRP, lipase, and triglycerides across glycemic stages. Functional experiments further demonstrated that uric acid lowered the threshold for inflammatory cytokine-induced mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, and β-cell apoptosis. Pharmacological interruption of the uric acid-IL-1 inflammatory axis restored mitochondrial function and preserved β-cell viability.
Hyperuricemia acts as a metabolic primer that sensitizes β-cells to cytokine-induced toxicity, precipitating irreversible mitochondrial collapse. Targeting this synergistic UA-inflammation axis offers a vital therapeutic strategy to preserve functional β-cell mass and mitigate type 2 diabetes-associated infectious complications.

articles.titulo: A standardized mosquito-to-mouse transmission assay with spatially defined bite areas
articles.autores: Miot EF, Medkour H, … Pompon J (10 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Mosquito-borne viruses initiate infection in the skin, where interactions between viral particles, host cells, and mosquito saliva can influence early infection and subsequent viral dissemination. Investigating these events requires methods that link mosquito exposure to the precise site of inoculation. However, identifying individual bite sites during subsequent tissue collection remains a practical challenge in mosquito-to-mouse transmission models. Here, we describe a standardized mosquito-to-mouse transmission assay that facilitates the localization of mosquito bite sites and targeted tissue sampling. The method combines a custom 3D-printed feeding device, individual mosquito exposure, and perforated adhesive tape to define the biting area and mark identified bite sites for subsequent collection. We demonstrate the application of this protocol using West Nile virus (WNV) and Dengue virus (DENV)-infected Aedes aegypti mosquitoes with C57BL/6J mice and A129 Ifnar1-/- mice, respectively. All infected mosquitoes successfully blood-fed within 20 min of exposure. After three infected-mosquito bites, mice developed clinical signs from approximately day 6 post-bite, with mortality occurring between days 8 and 10 for WNV, while disease onset occurred at 4 days post bite and most of the mice recovered by day 10 for DENV. To investigate early WNV viral kinetics in skin, WNV genomic RNA was quantified in biopsies collected at marked bite sites and the draining inguinal lymph nodes. Viral RNA was detected in both tissues as early as 1 h post-bite, and RNA levels increased significantly at 24 h post-bite. This protocol provides a practical approach for identifying mosquito bite sites and investigating early tissue-level events following vector-mediated transmission. With appropriate validation, the protocol can be adapted to other vector pathogen host systems and downstream analyses.

articles.titulo: Structural basis of Anopheles mosquito salivary protein complexes implicated in malaria transmission
articles.autores: Su T, Liu S, … Zhou ZH (5 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Successful malaria transmission by Anopheles mosquitoes depends on Plasmodium development within the mosquito midgut and subsequent sporozoite invasion of its salivary glands. Salivary proteins, notably Saglin and likely salivary gland surface proteins (SGS4 and SGS5), were suggested to play roles in these processes, but the lack of their structures has hindered our understanding of the underlying molecular mechanisms. In this study, we carried out biochemical and mass spectrometry analyses of salivary gland extracts and demonstrate that Anopheles gambiae SGS4 and SGS5 bind Saglin and other SG1 (salivary gland 1) proteins. Cryo-EM structure of the Saglin-SGS4 complex reveals that Saglin homodimerizes through coiled-coil interactions and disulfide bonds and engages longitudinally with SGS4. Comparisons among SG1-SGS complexes show that SG1 proteins share a conserved architecture, and SGS proteins adapt conformationally to bind different SG1 partners of varying lengths. To our knowledge, our findings uncover the first native mosquito salivary protein complexes that likely facilitate malaria transmission and highlight potential vector targets for blocking malaria transmission.

articles.titulo: THERM-D uncovers distinct neural mechanisms separating morning and evening body temperature rhythms in Drosophila
articles.autores: Goda T, Lopez OM, … Hamada FN (19 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Animal body temperature rises throughout the day and peaks in the evening, a pattern conserved across diurnal endotherms and ectotherms. However, the mechanisms driving the robust body temperature rhythms (BTRs) remain largely unclear. Here, we developed a machine learning-based platform, Temperature Homeostasis Evaluation of Rhythmicity in Model Drosophila (THERM-D), enabling continuous, high-throughput analyses of BTR. Using THERM-D, we identified robust BTR patterns reflecting flies' morning and evening behaviors and revealed the function of CRYPTOCHROME (CRY)-negative clock neurons. About half of all clock neurons lack CRY, yet their functions are only partially understood. Gal4 drivers targeting CRY-negative neurons demonstrated that these neurons control the morning temperature rise. We further show that separate clock circuits regulate morning and evening BTRs. Thus, THERM-D elucidated the role of CRY-negative clock neurons in BTR and provides a powerful platform for uncovering mechanisms underlying circadian temperature homeostasis.

articles.titulo: A synaptic mitochondrion-ribbon-vesicle complex organizes photoreceptor neurotransmission
articles.autores: Wang F, Zhao W, … Zhang J (13 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Photoreceptor synapses rely on mitochondria, synaptic ribbons, and vesicles, yet how these elements integrate into functional units remains unclear. Here we show, using focused ion beam-scanning electron microscopy (FIB-SEM) and electrophysiology, that they form synaptic mitochondrion-ribbon-vesicle complexes (sMRVcs) with fundamentally different architectures in rods and cones. Rod spherules exhibit a strict 1:1 pairing of a single megamitochondrion with one ribbon, sustaining continuous glutamate release in darkness, whereas cone pedicles contain multiple distributed sMRVcs. Disrupting the mitochondrial anchor protein syntaphilin shifts this ratio to 2:1 in rods, with additional mitochondria recruited near the ribbon, and enhances synaptic transmission. In a retinal degeneration model, the sMRVc progressively disassembles before functional decline, with fragmented mitochondria, detached ribbons, and dispersed vesicles. We also identify non-ribbon release sites selectively targeting horizontal cells. These findings establish the sMRVc as a conserved structural-metabolic module whose subtype-specific organization reflects distinct visual demands and whose integrity is essential for synaptic health.

articles.titulo: Metabolic profiling of brain and cerebrospinal fluid in cerebral malaria
articles.autores: Sachdeva C, Forster R, … Daily JP (12 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Cerebral malaria (CM), a severe neurological complication of Plasmodium falciparum infection, is a common cause of pediatric mortality and long-term cognitive impairment in endemic regions. The mechanisms driving CM-associated coma and neuropathology are not fully understood. We performed untargeted metabolomic profiling of brain tissue from experimental cerebral malaria (ECM) mouse models and brain autopsy tissue and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) samples from children with CM and non-malarial coma (NMC). ECM brain samples exhibited significant metabolic alterations, including differences in energy metabolism and amino acids and elevated pipecolic and lactic acids. In contrast, CM and NMC brain metabolomes showed limited differences. CSF metabolomes from cohorts in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Malawi showed elevated glyceric acid in CM compared with NMC. Together, these findings highlight metabolic perturbations in CM across species and sample types and identify glyceric acid as a potential CSF biomarker.

articles.titulo: The ACDC domains of AP2-O3 and FD3 contribute to protein interactions and ookinete development
articles.autores: Tang J, Liu B, … Li Z (7 autores)
articles.resumo_original: The Apicomplexan AP2 (ApiAP2) family of transcription factors are key regulators of Plasmodium spp. parasite development. In addition to containing AP2 DNA-binding domains, nine ApiAP2 proteins also encode an apicomplexan-specific ACDC domain whose function remains largely unknown. Here, we dissect the biological role of the ACDC domain from two female-specific regulators, AP2-O3 and FD3, using the rodent malaria model Plasmodium yoelii and the human malaria parasite P. falciparum. In Plasmodium yoelii, deletion of the ACDC domain preserved AP2-O3 and FD3 protein presence and nuclear localization without significantly affecting asexual growth or gametocyte production. However, deletion of these domains impaired the gametocyte-to-ookinete transition, reducing ookinete conversion efficiency. Proteomic and biochemical studies indicate that the AP2-O3 ACDC domain interacts with FD3, while the FD3 ACDC domain preferentially associates with full-length FD3. Transcriptomic data showed that over 80% of transcripts that increased after FD3 ACDC deletion were also higher following AP2-O3 loss, with female gametocyte marker expression largely unchanged. In Plasmodium falciparum, removing the FD3 ACDC domain did not affect female lineage-specific expression of FD3, nuclear localization of FD3, or the asexual growth and gametocyte maturation of parasites. Leveraging the high sequence conservation of ACDC domains across the Plasmodium genus, we conducted structure-based virtual screening of 283 compounds targeting the predicted PfAP2-O3 and PfFD3 ACDC interaction interface. Seven compounds ranked among the top candidate inhibitors for both domains, and the highest-priority ligand for each domain was further evaluated by molecular dynamics simulations. Collectively, our findings support a role for ACDC domains in ApiAP2 protein interactions and identify candidate compounds for future experimental evaluation as potential transmission-blocking leads.

articles.titulo: Estimating Culex species (Diptera: Culicidae) flight range: meta-analysis
articles.autores: Moore TC, Sedda L, … Brown HE (4 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Mosquitoes of the genus Culex transmit arboviruses of public health importance, including West Nile and Japanese encephalitis viruses. Dispersal, commonly measured as mean distance traveled (MDT), influences transmission dynamics and spatially targeted surveillance and control. However, Culex flight-distance estimates vary substantially because of differences in study design, environmental context, and analytical methods. We systematically synthesized empirical flight data and evaluated environmental and methodological factors associated with MDT across Culex species. A systematic literature review through December 2025 identified 206 experiments from 57 studies spanning 15 countries. MDT was estimated using nonweighted, capture-weighted, and inverse-variance weighted approaches. Multivariable generalized linear and mixed-effects models were applied to Culex tarsalis Coquillett, Cx. quinquefasciatus Say, Cx. pipiens L., and Cx. tritaeniorhynchus Giles, adjusting for study designs. Of 206 experiments, 119 were included in species-specific MDT estimations. Capture-weighted MDT was greatest for Cx. tarsalis (1,404 m; 95% CI: 865-2,281), followed by Cx. tritaeniorhynchus (347 m), Cx. quinquefasciatus (302 m), and Cx. pipiens (283 m). Study area radius was most consistently associated with estimation of the MDT, whereas recapture efficiency was inversely associated with the MDT. Environmental and methodological factors, including mosquito origin, release timing, temperature, and infrastructure, showed species-specific effects. Capture-weighted models produced more precise and stable estimates than inverse-variance approaches. These findings indicated that ecological and methodological factors influenced estimated Culex dispersal and emphasized the importance of accounting for study design when interpreting MDT. Species-specific estimates can improve spatial targeting of vector surveillance and control and inform arbovirus transmission models.

articles.titulo: Field video recording reveals how temperature and season influence Culex quinquefasciatus (Diptera: Culicidae) oviposition activity
articles.autores: Méndez-Cardona S, Schluep S, … Thongsripong P (4 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Understanding vector behaviors under natural field conditions is essential for refining targeted control strategies. Culex quinquefasciatus Say is an important vector of West Nile virus, yet fine-scale field oviposition dynamics across changing temperatures and seasons remain understudied, partly due to a lack of field monitoring tools. In this study, we developed an infrared video monitoring method that can be paired with oviposition traps. We deployed this monitoring system during summer and fall in coastal Florida to quantify the timing and duration of individual oviposition events relative to sunset and ambient temperature. Egg rafts were collected and reared to confirm species identity. Culex quinquefasciatus oviposition activity was concentrated within the early scotophase in both seasons. However, temporal patterns differed between sampling periods: summer oviposition was broadly dispersed across multiple hours of the night, whereas oviposition during the cooler fall occurred within a narrower window following dusk. Temperature was associated with oviposition behavior, with higher temperatures significantly associated with a greater frequency of observed oviposition events and shorter oviposition durations. Our findings demonstrate that the infrared video monitoring system can detect natural oviposition events in nighttime field conditions. We also found that oviposition dynamics vary with seasonal changes in temperature and sunset timing under natural field conditions. By identifying periods when gravid females are most actively visiting oviposition sites, these findings may help inform the timing of surveillance and targeted vector control activities such as adulticide applications during high-risk arboviral transmission periods.

articles.titulo: The chromosomal genome sequence of the malaria mosquito, Anopheles oryzalimnetes Wilkerson & Motoki, 2009
articles.autores: Sallum MAM, Bergo ES, … Lawniczak MKN (10 autores)
articles.resumo_original: We present a genome assembly from an individual female Anopheles oryzalimnetes (Arthropoda; Insecta; Diptera; Culicidae). The primary assembly has a total length of 178.36 megabases. Most of the primary assembly (99.39%) is scaffolded into 3 chromosomal pseudomolecules, including the X sex chromosome. The mitochondrial genome has also been assembled, with a length of 15.42 kilobases. This assembly was generated as part of the Anopheles Reference Genomes Project.
